paras: The Liberty vagrancy auction was the public sale of three Black people at Liberty, Bedford County, Virginia, on December 13, 1880, under an old state vagrancy law, by order of a magistrate. The buyers paid about $4 apiece for a term of up to three months, and a county judge freed the three on habeas corpus within days. Papers across the country carried the story, some as a sign of slavery's return and others as a joke about falling prices.

According to a Richmond special to the Chicago Tribune, the three had been "living on the county" for some time, and the law allowed people unable to support themselves to be sold to the highest bidder for ninety days. Interviewed in Lynchburg, County Judge M. Davis said they had been prosecuted for vagrancy before Justice J. W. McCormick, a Liberty hotel keeper, and ordered "hired out for three months at public vendue."

The sale took place at 11 a.m. near the courthouse green before what the Tribune called a large crowd of white and Black onlookers. The auctioneer, described as a man who had once sold slaves, praised the men's teeth and condition; the Tribune put their ages at about 28, 40 and 65, and quoted the oldest as saying it was the fifth time he had been sold. A Minnesota brief added that bidders thumped the men's chests and examined their eyes and teeth.

The wire from Lynchburg said there were few bidders and that the three were "knocked down" for $4 each, "charity for their destitute condition" being the bidders' motive. Judge Davis named the buyers as John Scott and Daniel Early, whom he said acted from charity and were probably asked to bid by "respectable" Black residents.

Black residents hired the lawyer H. C. Lowery and appealed to Circuit Judge Wingfield, who ruled that he had no jurisdiction over the magistrate's decision. Their counsel then obtained a writ of habeas corpus, and Judge Davis discharged the three because they fell under none of the statute's five heads of vagrancy and the overseer of the poor had not presented the charge. Bedford dispatches said the three were then welcomed "in every colored house" as martyrs, and that many Black Virginians feared the sale was a step toward reenslavement.

A Washington special reported fears among Black Virginians that the law would be used against Black men who supported the Republicans or the Mahone ticket. No report of a prosecution of anyone involved in the sale appears in the coverage.

The first reports came from a Lynchburg wire, printed on December 15 by the New York Sun and relayed widely, sometimes under headlines such as "Slavery Days Returned" and "Human Beings Sold." The Chicago Tribune gave the fullest coverage, headed "The Auction Block," "Sold into Slavery" and "Slavery," and its Washington correspondent warned of a "Bourbon program" to reenslave Black voters.

The Richmond Dispatch, by contrast, called the affair "insignificant in itself" and worried mainly about the use "the Radicals of the North" might make of it. Short items in Southern and Western papers turned the price into a racist joke: the Knoxville Daily Chronicle wrote that "Negroes are getting cheap in Virginia," and the Baptist Courier that "The price has fallen since 1861." Briefs on the sale ran into January 1881, and a smaller number of papers reported the release.

The Lynchburg wire and the Tribune described three men, but Judge Davis said one of the three was a woman. The Knoxville paper gave the term as two months rather than three, and reports differed on whether $4 was paid for each person or for the group. The Dispatch implied the release followed a hearing on Wednesday, December 15, while the Bedford dispatches said the three were freed on December 18.

accounts.gist: Three men sold at Liberty by a magistrate's order under an old vagrant law, ownership ending in three months, for $4 each, with charity the bidders' motive.

accounts.label: Tribune Richmond special
accounts.gist: An 11 a.m. auction before a mixed crowd, with an auctioneer who had sold slaves praising the men's teeth and condition; the lot went to one buyer.

accounts.label: County judge (interview)
accounts.gist: Judge Davis called the matter insignificant but unfortunate; one of the three was a woman, the buyers acted from charity, and he freed them on habeas corpus.

accounts.label: Bedford dispatch
accounts.gist: Black residents were alarmed, hired counsel and won release after a failed appeal; the three were freed on Dec. 18.

framing.detail: The Chicago Tribune headed its reports 'The Auction Block' and 'Sold into Slavery' and its Washington special warned of a 'Bourbon program' to reenslave Black voters.
The Richmond Dispatch, quoting Judge Davis, called the affair insignificant, praised the buyers' charity and worried about 'the handle which the Radicals of the North' might make of it.
Most papers ran the Lynchburg wire or a one-line brief, some under headlines such as 'Slavery Days Returned' and 'Human Beings Sold'.
Several briefs made racist jokes about price, from 'Negroes are getting cheap in Virginia' to 'The price has fallen since 1861.'
